title: Two-Dimensional Phase Transitions in Classical Systems: 60 Years after the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner Theorem
abstract: In 1966, Hohenberg, Mermin and Wagner proved that long-wavelength fluctuations destabilize the long-range order of continuous symmetry in two-dimensional (2D) systems. Later in the 1970s, Berezinskii, Kosterlitz and Thouless developed the BKT theory describing an unconventional phase transition between quasi-long-range and short-range order in 2D systems driven by the binding-unbinding of topological defects, which has become a fundamental topic in statistical mechanics, condensed matter physics, and soft matter physics. One of the most important applications of the BKT theory is the melting of 2D crystals, whose mechanisms are not yet fully understood. Recently, this topic has been extended to the area of active matter, where the non-equilibrium nature leads to novel phenomena that deviate from the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem. In this review, we first focus on the recent theoretical and computational progress in the 2D melting problem in passive systems, and then summarize the inspiring results obtained from non-equilibrium systems. The review closes with comments on several promising directions for predicting 2D melting scenarios and for understanding the non-equilibrium nature in 2D active matter systems.
summary: This review surveys the theoretical landscape of 2D phase transitions, detailing established concepts like the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition. It critically updates this knowledge by incorporating recent findings on how non-equilibrium active matter systems deviate from these classical predictions, pointing toward new avenues for understanding melting.
main_problem: The review comprehensively analyzes two-dimensional (2D) phase transitions, focusing on the BKT transition and crystal melting, while extending the discussion to non-equilibrium active matter systems.
main_result: The paper contrasts equilibrium predictions (like HMW and BKT theory) with novel phenomena observed in active matter, suggesting that non-equilibrium dynamics fundamentally alter the expected phase transition behavior.
method: It synthesizes results from Renormalization Group (RG) theory, continuum descriptions of topological defects (Coulomb gas), finite-size scaling analysis, and comparisons between different thermodynamic ensembles (NVT vs NPT).
model_or_system: The primary models include the XY spin model for continuous symmetry breaking, 2D crystalline solids undergoing melting, hard disk systems, and active Brownian particles (ABPs) in non-equilibrium settings.

main_assumptions: The review notes that early theories rely on continuum descriptions, and numerical simulations are limited by finite-size effects and critical slowing down.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate topological defects in spin systems and 2D crystals; one figure shows the calculation of translational correlation functions via reciprocal vector scanning; another details phase diagrams for hard polygons showing various melting routes (e.g., $	ext{S} 	o 	ext{TX} 	o 	ext{R}_X$).
paper_structure: The review progresses logically from foundational theory (HMW/BKT) to detailed analysis of passive systems (melting via KTHNY), then explores the influence of particle shape and interaction potential range, culminating in a discussion of non-equilibrium active matter.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial bridge between classical equilibrium statistical mechanics (like BKT theory) and modern non-equilibrium physics, which is highly relevant for understanding complex many-body dynamics far from equilibrium.
